name: CSS Communications

profile.address: 1911, C Street, Lettered Streets, Bellingham, Whatcom County, Washington, 98225
profile.reading:
CSSNW Bellingham is a colocation and data center facility at 1911 C Street in Bellingham, Washington, operated by CSS Integration and Communications, Inc., a locally based Pacific Northwest company that combines colocation hosting with fiber connectivity, managed IT and cloud services, and offsite backup for businesses across Whatcom County and the wider region. Rather than building one large data hall for a single anchor tenant, CSS designs the facility around flexible, small-footprint colocation. Customers can rent hosting for a single server, a half cabinet, a full cabinet, or a multi-rack cage, a model that fits a company whose core customer base is regional businesses needing a secure, professionally run place to keep their own equipment rather than large enterprise or hyperscale tenants.

The operator's own facilities page describes real infrastructure at the site rather than generic marketing language. Fire protection is handled by an FM-200 clean-agent suppression system, which extinguishes fires without water damage to server equipment, standard practice for data halls. Backup power comes from an onsite natural-gas generator, and the facility offers 110V, 208V, and negative 48V DC power options, the DC option being the kind of power telecom carrier-grade equipment typically requires, a detail that signals CSS serves telecom and network customers alongside standard IT colocation clients. Redundant HVAC systems maintain environmental control, and physical security includes 24-hour card-key access with alarm monitoring and staffing during business hours. Support staff can perform hands-on tasks ranging from a simple reboot to a full server rebuild for clients whose own offices are unstaffed outside business hours.

Connectivity is one of the facility's stronger selling points for a market this size. It connects to a wide set of regional and national carriers, including Noel Communications, Integra Telecom, Blackrock Cable, Wave Broadband, Wolfe Internet, Comcast, AT&T, CenturyLink, Open Access, PogoZone, and Opalco Internet, giving Bellingham-area tenants a genuine choice of upstream providers inside a single building rather than being locked into one.

What CSS does not publish is any figure for total IT capacity, floor area, or a formal uptime or design-tier certification. That omission is ordinary for a facility of this kind. CSS is a regional colocation and managed-services provider serving a market well below the scale where publishing megawatt or Tier ratings functions as a competitive marketing tool, and its public materials are aimed at prospective tenants who care about price, hands-on support, and carrier choice rather than data-center benchmarking against national or hyperscale operators.

reading:
CSS Communications is the shorthand this registry inherited for CSS Integration and Communications, Inc., a Bellingham, Washington company founded in 1988 by Ray Poorman, who still serves as its president and chief technology officer. It is a regional carrier and integrator rather than a data centre developer, and its colocation business grew out of the network it already ran. The company describes more than two decades of last mile work for residential and business customers across the north west corner of Washington, including partnerships with regional ports and municipalities and current projects extending service to the Lummi Nation and to Guemes Island in cooperation with San Juan Cable. That is the useful frame for this record. The colocation space exists because the fibre was already there, not the other way round.

The registry holds one facility, at 1911 C Street in Bellingham, which is also the company's corporate address. The company markets it as one of the most connected buildings in Whatcom County. It sells space from a single server through partial cabinets to full 46U cabinets and multi rack cages, with 110 volt, 208 volt and minus 48 volt DC power options, redundant uninterruptible power supplies, redundant air conditioning, FM 200 clean agent fire suppression and card key access. The carrier list it publishes is regional and specific, naming Noel Communications, Integra Telecom, Blackrock Cable, Wave Broadband, Comcast fibre, AT and T fibre and CenturyLink fibre among others, and the company holds its own ARIN address space and runs BGP, which is what allows it to sell genuinely provider independent connectivity to a small customer base.

Two things about this operator are commonly misreported. The first is scope. The company's own site describes three colocation locations rather than one, the Bellingham building, a Burlington site to the south that was under construction and sits on a fibre ring toward Seattle, and space in the Westin Building in Seattle with access to the Seattle Internet Exchange. Only Bellingham is in this registry. The second is standby power. The company states that its backup generation is natural gas fired rather than diesel, which it describes as giving effectively unlimited run time because the fuel is piped rather than stored. That is a statement about standby generation and fuel supply, and it says nothing about how much computing load the building can carry. No critical IT capacity, no utility service size and no generator megawatt rating has been published for 1911 C Street, and there is no on site generation in the sense of a fuel cell or turbine plant serving the load in normal operation.

The building itself is mapped as retail construction and carries a telephone company style location code in the map data, which fits a downtown structure that has been adapted rather than purpose built. No square footage, year of conversion or ownership record for the building has been located, and the third party listings that describe the site carry a marketing arrangement with a Phoenix based colocation broker that some sources have misread as a parent company relationship. On the evidence available the two are separate, one selling space and the other listing it.

Bellingham is an unusual place to find carrier neutral colocation. It sits about twenty miles from the Canadian border, well outside the Seattle metro, and the market it serves is county sized. That is the interesting thing about this record. It is what independent regional infrastructure looks like when it survives, small, closely held, thirty five years old and built around fibre the owner laid himself.
